title: Y-D-A
carry: to know is to be close

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ch-N-N: chen, grace, the favor Noah found. Your line was grace. Were you gracious once, to someone who didn't expect it? Today, a root about knowing. Day one thousand three hundred eighty-two.

A doctor can know your chart cover to cover and still not know you. A neighbor of many years can know your name, your car and the morning you take out the trash, and nothing else. English uses one verb for all of it and doesn't blink. Hebrew has a verb for knowing too, and in the Bible it keeps turning up where English would reach for a warmer word. A garden. A marriage. A name spoken by God. Today's root is three letters, yud, dalet, ayin: Y-D-A. And it carries a simple question. What does it take to really know someone?
screen: `THE CHART, NOT THE PERSON.` → `ONE VERB IN ENGLISH.` → `Y-D-A: TO KNOW.`

segments.voice: Y-D-A gives the verb yada, to know, and the noun da'at, knowledge. Turn it four ways. First, the garden. In Genesis, a tree stands in the middle of Eden called "the tree of the knowledge of good and evil." Knowledge there is da'at. In the story it isn't something you look up. It's something you take in, eat, and carry inside you. Second, the marriage. Two chapters later the same verb turns up where some readers don't expect it: "And the man knew Eve his wife." Yada, for the closest two people can be. In the Bible's Hebrew, knowing can mean intimacy. Third, the name. Moses asks to be shown God's ways, and the answer comes back: "thou hast found grace in My sight, and I know thee by name." Grace, yesterday's word, sits right beside knowing. To be known by name, here, is to be held close, not filed away. Fourth, the hope. The prophet Jeremiah describes a day when no one will need to teach a neighbor about God, "for they shall all know Me, from the least of them unto the greatest of them." Not know about. Know. Some Jewish teachers read that knowing as a relationship more than a fact, the way you know a friend's laugh from across a crowded room. So whenever this root appears, it brings a question along: is this knowing at arm's length, or up close? The neighbor who knows your trash day has information. The friend who can tell why you're quiet today has da'at.
screen: `THE GARDEN: DA'AT, KNOWLEDGE.` · `THE MARRIAGE: THE MAN KNEW EVE.` · `THE NAME: I KNOW THEE BY NAME.` · `THE HOPE: THEY SHALL ALL KNOW ME.` · then, large: `יָדַע`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: get to know someone better, starting now. Settle, and breathe. Bring one person to mind, someone you see often but know only at arm's length. A coworker, a cousin, the person behind the counter. Notice what you actually know: a name, a face, a habit. Then notice what you don't. What makes them laugh. Who they miss. How their week has really gone. Choose one question you could ask them, a real one, and hold it gently. If you pray, you can bring their name with you into the quiet. The bell holds the time.
Y-D-A. Yud, dalet, ayin: the root of yada, to know, and da'at, knowledge, where knowing can mean closeness. Today's word.
Your line: to know is to be close. Today, ask one person your real question, and listen all the way to the end of the answer. Day one thousand three hundred eighty-two.

howItsDone: Some Jewish teachers note that the Hebrew verb yada, to know, is used in the Bible for intimacy and relationship as well as for facts, and da'at, knowledge, is a word that recurs in Jewish prayer and study.
